Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The Indian cobra is an elapine snake, and cobra venom is characteristically neurotoxic, paralysing the respiratory centre.
  • The Indian krait is likewise an elapine with predominantly neurotoxic venom, not haemotoxic.
  • Since Russell's viper does fit the description, stating that none of the four fits is incorrect.
Know More
  • The four common poisonous snakes of India are the Indian cobra, Indian krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.
  • Of roughly 3,500 species of snakes, only about 400 belonging to six families are venomous.
  • Elapine bites cause minimal local pain/swelling but predominant systemic neurologic signs, while viper bites cause severe local tissue damage.
  • Use of a tourniquet, incision and suction, cryotherapy and surgical debridement are generally contraindicated in snakebite management.

posts.post_title: Tetrodotoxin, the potent neurotoxin of puffe…
posts.post_content: Tetrodotoxin, found concentrated in the liver, skin and intestine of pufferfish, causes paralysis by affecting the transport of which ion?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sodium

Tetrodotoxin causes paralysis by affecting sodium ion transport in both the central and peripheral nervous systems.

Correct Option Explanation

A low dose produces tingling and numbness around the mouth, fingers and toes, while higher doses cause nausea, vomiting, respiratory failure and extensive paralysis; it is one of the most potent known toxins, with an acute lethal dose of about 0.01 mg/kg.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Calcium ion transport is instead relevant to the mechanism of black widow spider venom, not tetrodotoxin.
  • Potassium ion transport is not the mechanism described for tetrodotoxin's paralytic action.
  • Chloride ion transport is central to GABA receptor action (e.g. avermectins), not tetrodotoxin.
Know More
  • Both tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin are heat stable, so cooking does not reduce their toxicity.
  • Saxitoxin is also produced by algae and is responsible for paralytic shellfish poisoning.
  • Saxitoxin has a similar mechanism but is less toxic than tetrodotoxin.
  • Conotoxins from cone snails also interfere with neuronal communication, targeting nicotinic receptors, sodium and calcium channels.

posts.post_title: In snake envenomation therapy, which measure…
posts.post_content: In the therapeutic management of snake envenomation, which of the following measures is generally considered contraindicated?

_aimcq_options.text: Administration of specific or polyvalent antivenom
Broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent secondary infection

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Use of a tourniquet

Tourniquet use is controversial and generally avoided in snakebite management, as it increases local tissue damage due to hypoxia.

Correct Option Explanation

Tourniquets are recommended only when the tissue below them will be sacrificed to save the animal's life; other contraindicated therapies include incision and suction, cryotherapy and surgical debridement.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Administration of specific antivenom (or polyvalent antivenom if the species is unknown) is a recommended, not contraindicated, treatment objective.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics are recommended given the range of pathogens isolated from snakes' mouths such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • Fluid therapy is generally indicated, especially in small animals, since hypotension is a common presenting sign.
Know More
  • Envenomation is possible even after a poisonous snake has been decapitated, so caution is required even with a dead snake.
  • Alcohol should not be used to clean the wound due to its vasodilatory effect, which promotes venom spread.
  • Tetanus antitoxin should always be given to an affected horse.
  • Corticosteroid use in snakebite is controversial and has been associated with increased mortality in some reports.

posts.post_title: Withdrawal time is defined as the time from
posts.post_content: The withdrawal time of a veterinary drug is defined as the time from which point to when residues decline below a safe concentration?

_aimcq_options.text: The start of treatment to peak drug concentration
The cessation of treatment to the residues declining below the safe concentration
Birth of the animal to slaughter
The onset of clinical signs to full recovery

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The cessation of treatment to the residues declining below the safe concentration

Withdrawal time is defined as the time from the cessation of treatment to the time it takes for drug residues to deplete below the safe concentration.

Correct Option Explanation

It is based on the time for an average human to ingest 1/100 or 1/2000 of the NOEL, and withdrawal times are specific to species, dose, route, frequency of administration, manufacturer and formulation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Withdrawal time is measured relative to cessation of treatment, not the start of treatment or peak concentration.
  • It is not defined relative to the animal's birth, but to the specific treatment event.
  • It concerns drug residue depletion in edible tissues, not the clinical course of recovery from disease.
Know More
  • Meat withdrawal periods range from 0 to 60 days depending on the product, e.g. no withdrawal for ceftiofur but 28 days for pirlimycin.
  • Milk withdrawal examples include 36 hours for pirlimycin and 72 hours for penicillin.
  • Safe concentration is calculated as (ADI × 60 kg) / (500 g × Food factor).
  • MRL (Maximum Residue Limit) must be established for edible tissues; absence of an MRL is treated as equivalent to an MRL of zero.

posts.post_title: Which body is responsible for developing int…
posts.post_content: Which international body was established to develop international standards for food, protecting consumer health while ensuring fair trade practices?

_aimcq_options.text: Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of the USA

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Codex Alimentarius Commission

The Codex Alimentarius Commission is the international body established to develop international standards for food.

Correct Option Explanation

It aims to protect the health of consumers while ensuring fair practices in the food trade; related to this framework is the HACCP (Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point) system, which emphasises prevention of food safety problems.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • WHO is a relevant global health body but is not specifically the commission named for setting international food standards in this context.
  • The International Atomic Energy Agency deals with nuclear/radiation matters, not food standards.
  • The FDA is a national (US) regulatory agency, not an international standard-setting body.
Know More
  • HACCP has three parts: hazard identification, determination of critical control points (CCP), and monitoring procedures.
  • A critical control point is a location or process used to minimise or prevent unacceptable contamination or hazard introduction.
  • ADI (Acceptable Daily Intake) is the amount of residue that can be ingested for a lifetime without deleterious health effects.
  • NOEL is the highest dosage level producing no observable morphologic or functional change in test animals.

posts.post_title: Radium's toxic effect in the historical 'rad…
posts.post_content: In the historic radium dial-painters' poisoning cases, radium ingested via paintbrush-pointing caused disease mainly because of its

_aimcq_options.text: Long half-life combined with sequestration in bone, causing lifetime alpha radiation exposure
Conversion to a non-radioactive isotope in the liver
Immediate acute lethal dose on first exposure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Long half-life combined with sequestration in bone, causing lifetime alpha radiation exposure

Radium's long half-life combined with its sequestration in bone resulted in a lifetime of radiation exposure for the affected dial painters.

Correct Option Explanation

Radium ingested via brush-pointing moved to the bone, where it continued to emit alpha radiation, damaging nearby cells and leading to painfully debilitating bone decay and cancer over the women's lifetimes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rapid excretion is the opposite of what occurred — radium was retained and sequestered in bone rather than excreted.
  • Radium is not described as converting to a non-radioactive isotope; it remained radioactive and continued emitting radiation.
  • The disease developed gradually over years of exposure, not from a single immediate lethal dose.
Know More
  • These radium dial painters were among the first to receive compensation for occupational injury after suing in the 1920s.
  • Alpha particles are shielded by paper or a layer of skin but are the primary hazard from internal exposure.
  • Marie Curie discovered radium in 1898 and shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.
  • Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the first Nobel Prize in physics in 1901.

posts.post_title: Which type of radiation is most hazardous wh…
posts.post_content: Alpha particles from radionuclides are most dangerous by which route of exposure?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhalation and/or ingestion (internal exposure)

Alpha particles released by radionuclides are dangerous if taken into the body by inhalation and/or ingestion.

Correct Option Explanation

Alpha particles have a charge of +2 and transfer energy over very short distances (about 10 cm in air) and are shielded by paper or a layer of skin, so external exposure is minimal, but once internalised they become a serious internal radiation source, as seen with radon-induced lung cancer.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alpha particles are readily blocked by external barriers like clothing and skin, making external exposure comparatively minor.
  • Reflection off surfaces is not a mechanism of alpha particle hazard described in the source material.
  • Alpha particles are easily shielded even by paper, so thick lead shielding is unnecessary for external protection; the hazard is specifically internal.
Know More
  • Alpha emitters can accumulate in tissues such as bone, kidney, liver, lung and spleen, causing local damage.
  • Gamma rays are highly penetrating and require extensive shielding, posing a serious external radiation hazard.
  • Reducing radiation exposure relies on time, distance and shielding.
  • Very high radiosensitivity tissues include white blood cells (bone marrow), intestinal epithelium and reproductive cells.

posts.post_title: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984 was caused by…
posts.post_content: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy, one of the world's worst industrial catastrophes, resulted from the leakage of which chemical?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Methyl isocyanate

The Bhopal disaster resulted from a leak of methylisocyanate gas and other chemicals from the Union Carbide India Pesticide Plant.

Correct Option Explanation

It occurred on the night of 2-3 December 1984 in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh; inhalation of large quantities of this highly irritant substance causes immediate bronchoconstriction and pulmonary oedema, a locally mediated rather than systemic effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Chlorine gas was not the chemical responsible for the Bhopal tragedy, though it is a known industrial hazard elsewhere.
  • Phosgene is a distinct toxic industrial/war gas not identified as the Bhopal disaster agent.
  • Sulphur dioxide causes laryngeal spasm and lung damage but was not the agent involved at Bhopal.
Know More
  • The official immediate death toll at Bhopal was 2,259, with the Madhya Pradesh government confirming a total of 3,787 deaths.
  • The Chernobyl disaster (1986) involved release of radioactive contamination, a distinct type of industrial catastrophe.
  • Industrial exposure occurs mainly via inhalation and skin contact, alongside oral ingestion.
  • Parathion is an insecticide that causes fatal poisoning following skin absorption in occupational settings.

posts.post_title: Asbestos exposure is specifically linked to…
posts.post_content: Chronic occupational exposure to asbestos fibres is specifically linked to which cancer, in addition to asbestosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mesothelioma

Asbestos causes lung cancer, specifically mesothelioma and bronchial carcinoma, along with the chronic lung disease asbestosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Asbestos fibres lodge in the lungs and are taken up by phagocytic cells, which then leak cell contents and damage surrounding tissue; fibre size is a crucial factor determining toxicity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bladder cancer is instead linked to aromatic amines like 2-naphthylamine, particularly in slow acetylators, not asbestos.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma is not the cancer type specifically associated with asbestos in this source; vinyl chloride is instead linked to rare liver cancer.
  • Osteosarcoma/bone tumours are instead associated with exposure to radon, radium and uranium, not asbestos.
Know More
  • Cadmium toxicity causes kidney damage, brittle bones (Itai-Itai disease) and, after chronic inhalation, lung irritation and emphysema.
  • Nickel and its salts are a well-known cause of contact dermatitis ('nickel itch').
  • 2-Naphthylamine can be detoxified by acetylation; slow acetylators are at higher risk of bladder cancer.
  • Occupational exposure to chromium is linked to lung and nasal sinus cancer in process and pigment workers.

posts.post_title: Which classes of food additives are correctl…
posts.post_content: Which of the following correctly pairs a class of food additive with its representative example?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Colouring agent - Tartrazine

Tartrazine is correctly matched as a colouring agent.

Correct Option Explanation

Tartrazine, a common colouring agent, may lead to effects such as urticaria in susceptible individuals, illustrating that even long-approved food additives can carry specific risks in some people.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Monosodium glutamate is actually classed as a flavour enhancer, not a sweetener (saccharin is the listed sweetener example).
  • Sodium nitrate is actually classed as a preservative, not an anti-caking agent (magnesium carbonate is the listed anti-caking example).
  • Saccharin is actually classed as a sweetener, not a flavour enhancer (monosodium glutamate is the listed flavour-enhancer example).
Know More
  • Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) is a representative anti-oxidant food additive.
  • Testing the sweetener saccharin at high doses in animals led to bladder tumours, difficult to interpret given saturated elimination kinetics at high doses.
  • Benzoyl peroxide is used as a bleach-type food additive.
  • Not all toxicants in food are synthetic; many naturally occurring toxicants, including carcinogens, also exist in the diet.

posts.post_title: Which type of pigment metabolism disorder un…
posts.post_content: Bovine congenital erythropoietic porphyria and bovine erythropoietic protoporphyria fall under which classification of photosensitization?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aberrant endogenous pigment synthesis (type II)

Bovine congenital erythropoietic porphyria and bovine erythropoietic protoporphyria fall under type II photosensitivity, due to aberrant endogenous pigment synthesis.

Correct Option Explanation

In this syndrome, the photosensitizing porphyrin agents are endogenous pigments arising from inherited or acquired defects in enzymes involved in haeme synthesis, occurring in both cattle and cats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Type I (primary) photosensitization involves agents absorbed unchanged from skin or gut, such as hypericin, not endogenous pigment synthesis defects.
  • Type III (secondary/hepatogenous) photosensitization involves accumulation of phylloerythrin due to impaired hepatobiliary excretion, a different mechanism from congenital pigment synthesis disorders.
  • Type IV (idiopathic) photosensitization has an unknown pathogenesis, distinct from the known enzymatic defect underlying type II disease.
Know More
  • In bovine congenital erythropoietic porphyria, discoloration of dentin, bone and urine often accompanies skin lesions.
  • Photodermatitis is the sole manifestation in bovine erythropoietic protoporphyria.
  • Secondary (type III) photosensitization is by far the most frequent type observed in livestock.
  • Examination of blood, faeces and urine for porphyrins can assist diagnosis of pigment-related photosensitivity.

posts.post_title: Molluscicidal use is a documented applicatio…
posts.post_content: Copper sulphate, in addition to being an antifungal agent in agriculture, is also used for which of the following purposes?

_aimcq_options.text: Rodenticide against zinc phosphide resistant rats

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Destruction of snails

Copper sulphate is widely used as an antifungal agent in agricultural practice and is also used in the destruction of snails.

Correct Option Explanation

It additionally finds a place in the treatment of parasitic gastritis in sheep; copper toxicity most seriously arises as an acute syndrome linked to a chronic excessive copper-to-molybdenum dietary ratio.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Copper sulphate is not used to treat thallium poisoning; diphenylthiocarbazone and Prussian blue serve that role instead.
  • Copper sulphate is not a chelating agent for lead; sodium calcium edetate and penicillamine serve that role.
  • Copper sulphate is not described as a rodenticide; it is instead used as a molluscicide and antifungal agent.
Know More
  • Soils and plants fertilised with poultry litter and swine manure tend to have higher copper content.
  • Bedlington terriers have a genetic defect causing excessive hepatic copper storage.
  • Faeces of animals with acute copper poisoning are characteristically deep green in colour, containing mucous.
  • Treatment includes d-penicillamine, calcium versenate and ammonium tetrathiomolybdate.

posts.post_title: Which mineral element is deposited in the sk…
posts.post_content: Which of the following metals is, along with fluorine and strontium, selectively deposited in skeletal tissue?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lead

Lead, along with fluorine and strontium, is selectively deposited in skeletal tissue.

Correct Option Explanation

This tissue distribution parallels calcium handling, with lead deposition and subsequent mobilisation from bone occurring similarly to calcium, forming the basis of the 'bone sink for lead'.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Iodine is instead selectively deposited in the thyroid, not the skeleton.
  • Mercury compounds (mercurials) are selectively deposited in the kidneys, not primarily in bone.
  • Paraquat is selectively deposited in the lungs, not skeletal tissue.
Know More
  • Arsenic is selectively deposited in hair and nails.
  • Halogenated hydrocarbons are selectively deposited in adipose tissue.
  • Primaquine is selectively deposited in the liver.
  • Selective tissue affinity does not necessarily indicate that pathological lesions will develop at that site, but it is important for toxicological analysis.

posts.post_title: The condition known as 'blind staggers' is a…
posts.post_content: 'Blind staggers', a subacute clinical syndrome involving in-coordination, circling and near-blindness, results from poisoning by which element?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Selenium

'Blind staggers' is the subacute form of selenium poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

It occurs due to ingestion of seleniferous plants, progressing through stages of poor appetite and aimless wandering to in-coordination, foreleg weakness, colic, near-blindness and eventually complete paralysis and death.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Molybdenum toxicity presents as teart/peat scours with a pacing gait, not blind staggers.
  • Fluoride toxicity (fluorosis) presents primarily with dental and skeletal lesions, not the blind staggers syndrome.
  • Copper toxicity presents with haemolytic crisis and gun-metal kidney, unrelated to blind staggers.
Know More
  • Chronic selenium poisoning is termed 'alkali disease', historically attributed to consumption of alkali waters.
  • Obligate indicator plants like Astragalus (locoweed) require large amounts of selenium (100-10,000 ppm) for growth.
  • In Ireland, selenium toxicity is known as 'dog murrain'.
  • Addition of copper to the diet is useful to prevent selenosis in chronic selenium toxicity.

posts.post_title: Which factor most increases toxicity in case…
posts.post_content: Which of the following dietary conditions most increases the toxicity of molybdenum in ruminants?

_aimcq_options.text: High dietary sulphate combined with low copper
High dietary copper combined with low sulphate

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: High dietary sulphate combined with low copper

High dietary sulphate content with low copper increases the toxicity of molybdenum.

Correct Option Explanation

When copper intake decreases, tolerance to molybdenum toxicity also decreases; the water-soluble form of molybdenum is more toxic, and molybdenum significantly reduces hepatic copper storage in sheep and cattle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • High copper with low sulphate is the opposite condition to that which increases molybdenum toxicity — adequate copper actually protects against it.
  • High dietary calcium is not identified as the factor increasing molybdenum toxicity in this source.

Know More
  • Cattle are less tolerant than sheep to molybdenum toxicity.
  • Young animals are more susceptible than old animals to molybdenum toxicosis.
  • Molybdenum forms complexes with catechols, producing a bacteriostatic effect on gastrointestinal bacteria.
  • Depigmentation of hair around the eyes gives a characteristic 'spectacled appearance' in affected animals.

posts.post_title: In diagnosing poisoning, a garlic odour of g…
posts.post_content: A garlic-like odour of the gastrointestinal contents or breath, useful in diagnosing poisoning, is characteristic of exposure to

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Phosphorus

A garlic odour of the breath and gastrointestinal contents is characteristic of phosphorus poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

This odour is a key diagnostic clue for phosphorus toxicosis, alongside violent vomiting, diarrhoea, and postmortem findings of severe gastroenteritis and black, tarry blood that fails to clot.

  • Cyanide poisoning is instead associated with a bitter almond odour of the breath and stomach contents.

  • Metaldehyde is instead associated with an acetaldehyde odour on the breath or in vomitus.
Know More
  • The colour of urine can also aid diagnosis: dark green after phenolic compounds, red after phenothiazine.
  • Blood colour clues include cherry red in carbon monoxide poisoning and chocolate brown in nitrite/chlorate poisoning.

  • Renal lesions are commonly produced by nephrotoxic agents such as mercury and lead.

posts.post_title: Which classification of toxicity is assigned…
posts.post_content: Under the dose-based classification of poison toxicity, compounds with a lethal dose of 1-50 mg/kg are classified as

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Highly toxic

Compounds with a lethal dose of 1-50 mg/kg are classified as highly toxic.

Correct Option Explanation

This scale progresses from extremely toxic (<1 mg/kg) through highly toxic (1-50 mg/kg), moderately toxic (50-500 mg/kg), slightly toxic (0.5-5 g/kg), practically non-toxic (5-15 g/kg), to relatively harmless (>15 g/kg).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Extremely toxic corresponds to a lower dose range of less than 1 mg/kg, not 1-50 mg/kg.
  • Moderately toxic corresponds to the higher range of 50-500 mg/kg, not 1-50 mg/kg.
  • Slightly toxic corresponds to an even higher range of 0.5-5 g/kg, well above the 1-50 mg/kg band.
Know More
  • Compounds requiring 5-15 g/kg to cause death are classified as practically non-toxic.
  • Compounds requiring more than 15 g/kg are classified as relatively harmless.
  • Nicotine and many plant poisons have lethal doses around 1 mg/kg.
  • Curare and sea snake venoms have lethal doses around 0.1 mg/kg.

posts.post_title: Sub-acute toxicity studies to determine the…

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Know More
  • Chronic toxicity studies run for six months to two years in rodents.
  • Sub-acute poisoning involves a lower exposure level and longer survival time than acute poisoning, but still a relatively short interval before signs manifest.
  • Toxicity testing types include acute, subchronic, chronic, developmental, reproductive, phototoxicity, behavioural and hypersensitivity testing.
  • Rodents are commonly used as experimental animals in many of these toxicity studies.

posts.post_title: Teratogenicity is best defined as
posts.post_content: Teratogenicity, a term derived from a Greek word meaning 'monster', is best defined as

_aimcq_options.text: An agent inducing uncontrolled cell proliferation after a delay
An agent that, when administered during gestation, produces nonlethal structural or functional changes in the embryo/fetus
An agent causing mutation through covalent modification of DNA bases
An agent causing allergic sensitization to a previous dose

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: An agent that, when administered during gestation, produces nonlethal structural or functional changes in the embryo/fetus

A teratogen is an agent which, when administered during gestation, produces nonlethal structural or functional changes in the embryo or fetus.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include plants like Veratrum and Lupinus and drugs like thalidomide and colchicine; exposure during certain critical stages of gestation to naturally occurring or man-made agents can result in such malformations.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Inducing uncontrolled cell proliferation after a delay describes carcinogenicity, a distinct untoward effect.
  • Mutation through covalent DNA modification describes mutagenicity, a separate concept from teratogenicity.
  • Sensitization to a previous dose describes allergy, unrelated to the teratogenic definition.
Know More
  • Carcinogenicity refers to an agent's ability to transform normal cells into progressively, uncontrollably proliferating ones after a delay.
  • Mutagenicity involves changes in the genotype through covalent modification of DNA bases, particularly affecting cell division.
  • Hemlock (Conium maculatum) can also produce teratogenic effects in offspring.
  • Epoxides formed during biotransformation can react with DNA and RNA, contributing to mutation and carcinogenesis.

posts.post_title: Which type of evidence is generally consider…
posts.post_content: Which category of evidence in the diagnosis of poisoning is specifically noted as being insufficient to serve, on its own, as the sole basis for diagnosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Circumstantial evidence

Circumstantial evidence cannot be the sole basis for a diagnosis of poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

It may instead help in assessing the direction in which further investigation should be conducted; sources include contaminated fittings, feed changes, agrochemical spraying of pastures, or nearby factories contaminating water and soil.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Historical evidence plays a major role, with veterinarians depending heavily on it for diagnosis, so it is not the type flagged as insufficient alone.
  • Pathological evidence, particularly characteristic gross or histopathological lesions, is a valuable diagnostic tool, especially in chronic poisoning.
  • Analytical evidence provides confirmatory laboratory data and is considered when there is sound evidence of poisoning with a known compound group.
Know More
  • Diagnosis of poisoning may be tentative, presumptive or confirmative.
  • Odour of breath diagnostic clues include phenolic (phenol), bitter almonds (cyanide) and garlic (phosphorus).
  • Ethanol is the best preservative if one is needed when sending samples for analysis.
  • Samples are usually best deep frozen as quickly as possible after collection.

posts.post_title: How much blood volume is typically required…
posts.post_content: For antemortem sample collection to detect exposure to most metals, trace elements, cholinesterase and pesticides, how much blood is typically recommended?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5-10 ml

Blood samples of 5-10 ml are useful for detecting exposure to most metals, trace elements, cholinesterase and pesticides.

Correct Option Explanation

Blood is also useful for evaluating erythrocyte and leucocyte morphology and for detecting exposure to ethylene glycol, providing a versatile antemortem sample for toxicological analysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1-2 ml is insufficient compared with the documented recommended volume of 5-10 ml.
  • 50 ml is instead the amount recommended for a urine sample, not blood.
  • 250 g is a mass, appropriate for faeces or vomitus samples, not a blood volume.
Know More
  • Urine (50 ml) is useful for detecting alkaloids, metals, electrolytes, antibiotics and oxalates.
  • Liver (100 g) is the major organ of biotransformation, accumulating metals, pesticides and alkaloids.
  • Hair (5-10 g) is useful for detecting dermal pesticide exposure and chronic accumulation of arsenic or selenium.
  • Fat (250 g) is useful for detecting cumulative fat-soluble toxicants like chlorinated pesticides and dioxins.

posts.post_title: Which site is the primary and most important…
posts.post_content: Following oral ingestion of a toxicant, which is described as the important site of absorption, with the large intestine also being important in non-ruminants?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Small intestine

The small intestine is the important site of absorption, while the large intestine is also important in non-ruminants.

Correct Option Explanation

Absorption from the stomach in dogs and from the rumen and reticulum in ruminants are also important sites; hydrochloric acid in the stomach can increase the solubility of certain poisons, thereby increasing absorption.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The oesophagus is a conduit for ingesta and is not identified as a significant site of toxicant absorption.
  • The rumen is an important absorption site specifically in ruminants, but the small intestine is identified as the important site generally, especially relevant in non-ruminants.
  • The reticulum is likewise important in ruminants specifically, not as the general primary absorption site across species.
Know More
  • Presence of feed in the stomach dilutes toxins and can delay intoxication, an effect greater in ruminants.
  • Constipation increases toxicity while diarrhoea decreases absorption of ingested poisons.
  • Solubility is the primary factor affecting absorption of a toxicant.
  • Absorption can also occur via the mammary gland, uterus and eye, in addition to pulmonary and cutaneous routes.

posts.post_title: Which two detoxification pathways does the l…
posts.post_content: In the normal course, the liver converts absorbed ammonia into which two products as detoxification mechanisms?

_aimcq_options.text: Urea via the urea cycle, and glutamine via glutamic acid synthesis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Urea via the urea cycle, and glutamine via glutamic acid synthesis

In the normal course, liver ammonia is converted into urea by the urea cycle or incorporated into glutamic acid in the synthesis of glutamine.

Correct Option Explanation

Both these detoxification processes are enzymatic and depend on substrates produced by the citric acid cycle; when ammonia levels are high, these saturable pathways cannot detoxify ammonia fast enough, leading to toxicity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Uric acid and creatinine are not the pathways described for hepatic ammonia detoxification in this context.
  • Nitrite and nitrate relate to a separate toxicant pathway (nitrate/nitrite poisoning), not ammonia detoxification.
  • Glucose and lactate are instead products of increased anaerobic glycolysis that occurs as a consequence of ammonia toxicity, not detoxification products of ammonia itself.
Know More
  • Increased ammonia leads to inhibition of the citric acid cycle, with a resultant increase in anaerobic glycolysis, blood glucose and blood lactate.
  • At rumen pH 6.2, most nitrogen exists as poorly absorbed NH4+ ions.
  • L-arginine and N-Carbamyl-L-glutamate can stimulate the urea cycle, though this treatment approach is of doubtful benefit.
  • Emptying the rumen provides prompt relief from urea toxicosis but is difficult to carry out practically.

posts.post_title: Which enzyme is targeted by arsenic through…
posts.post_content: Arsenic exerts its principal toxic mechanism by reacting with the sulphydryl group of which essential cofactor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lipoic acid

Arsenic reacts with the sulphydryl group of lipoic acid, an essential cofactor for enzymatic decarboxylation of keto acids.

Correct Option Explanation

By inactivating lipoic acid, arsenic inhibits formation of acetyl, succinyl and propionyl coenzyme A, slowing glycolysis and the citric acid cycle; it also inactivates sulphydryl groups of oxidative enzymes and glutathione.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coenzyme Q interaction is central to rotenone's mechanism (blocking electron transport between flavoprotein and ubiquinone), not arsenic's.
  • Cytochrome oxidase inhibition is the mechanism of cyanide toxicity, not arsenic.
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates and carbamates, unrelated to arsenic's mechanism.
Know More
  • Pentavalent arsenate is a well-known uncoupler of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Arsenic is a potent capillary poison, with splanchnic beds more sensitive.
  • Dimercaprol (BAL) binds arsenic to form a non-toxic arsenic-mercaptide complex that is easily excreted.
  • Thioctic acid (lipoic acid itself) can also be administered as supportive treatment in arsenic poisoning.

posts.post_title: Which factor most increases arsenic toxicity…
posts.post_content: Regarding the physical state of arsenic compounds, which form is associated with the greatest toxicity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Finely divided soluble forms

Finely divided soluble forms of arsenic are more toxic.

Correct Option Explanation

The rate of absorption of inorganic arsenicals from the digestive tract depends on their solubility, and soluble salts are more toxic and can also be absorbed through the skin, particularly rapidly from a fresh wound.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coarse powder forms are less readily absorbed and therefore less toxic than finely divided soluble forms.
  • Large solid lumps present less surface area for dissolution and absorption, reducing toxicity relative to finely divided forms.
  • Insoluble compounds are, by definition, poorly absorbed and hence less toxic than soluble forms.
Know More
  • Arsenic poisoning is more common in bovines and felines; it is occasional in dogs and rare in swine and poultry.
  • After absorption, arsenicals tend to accumulate in the liver, and with continued exposure, in bone, skin and keratinised tissue.
  • Weak, debilitated and dehydrated animals are more susceptible to arsenic toxicity.
  • Habitual use of small quantities of arsenic can render the body tolerant to much larger doses.

posts.post_title: Which of the following soluble lead salts is…
posts.post_content: Regarding lead compounds, which of the following statements about relative toxicity is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Insoluble salts like lead acetate are more toxic than lead oxide
Soluble salts like lead acetate are more toxic than insoluble salts like lead oxide
Lead oxide is more toxic than any soluble lead salt
Solubility has no bearing on lead toxicity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Soluble salts like lead acetate are more toxic than insoluble salts like lead oxide

Soluble salts of lead like lead acetate are more toxic than insoluble salts like lead oxide.

Correct Option Explanation

Lead acetate, known as 'sugar of lead', is an important soluble salt used in preparing white lotion; higher solubility generally correlates with greater absorption and toxicity, consistent with the general toxicological principle that solubility increases absorption.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This option incorrectly describes lead acetate as insoluble; it is in fact a well-known soluble salt of lead.
  • Lead oxide, being relatively insoluble, is less toxic than the soluble salts, not more.
  • Solubility is explicitly identified as an important factor influencing lead toxicity, contrary to this option.
Know More
  • Pregnant ewes are more susceptible to lead poisoning.
  • Goats, swine and chicken are relatively resistant to lead poisoning among domestic species.
  • Rate of ingestion matters: large amounts ingested over one or two days are more toxic than the same total dose spread out.
  • Sheep may acquire a taste for lead and preferentially graze high-contamination areas.

posts.post_title: Which anaemia-related mechanism underlies le…
posts.post_content: Lead produces anaemia principally by which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Inhibiting enzymes with free sulphydryl groups involved in haeme precursor synthesis
Blocking erythropoietin receptors in bone marrow
Competing with iron for transferrin binding

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibiting enzymes with free sulphydryl groups involved in haeme precursor synthesis

Lead produces toxicity by inhibiting enzymes with free sulphydryl groups, particularly precursors of haeme synthesis, causing anaemia.

Correct Option Explanation

Lead poisoning is characterised by accumulation of protoporphyrin IX and non-haeme iron in red blood cells, accumulation of aminolevulinate in plasma, and increased excretion of aminolevulinate; lead also inhibits haeme synthetase and prevents iron entry from cytosol to mitochondria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct haemolysis of mature erythrocytes is not the primary anaemia mechanism described for lead; the effect is on haeme synthesis machinery.
  • Blocking erythropoietin receptors is not a mechanism attributed to lead toxicity in this source.
  • Competing with iron for transferrin is not the described mechanism; lead instead prevents iron entry into mitochondria via a different pathway.
Know More
  • Level of lead >4 ppm in the liver or 0.2 ppm in whole blood indicates lead poisoning; twice these levels are fatal.
  • Basophilic stippling of red cells and nucleated RBCs are associated with lead poisoning in dogs.
  • Measurement of ALA dehydratase in blood aids diagnosis.
  • Differential diagnosis of nervous lead poisoning includes hypomagnesemic tetany, nervous acetonaemia and tetanus.

posts.post_title: The 'sardonic grin' and sawhorse stance are…
posts.post_content: The 'sardonic grin' and characteristic 'sawhorse stance' with generalized muscular rigidity are classic clinical features of which toxicosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both tetanus and strychnine poisoning

Both tetanus and strychnine poisoning produce a rigid, sawhorse-type stance with sustained muscular spasm, though tetanus specifically produces the 'sardonic grin'.

Correct Option Explanation

In tetanus, tetany is characterised by sustained tonic contraction without twitching, with a 'sardonic grin', protrusion of the third eyelid and rigidity; strychnine similarly produces continuous tetanic seizures with marked rigidity described as a 'sawhorse stance', reflecting their shared theme of loss of inhibitory neurotransmission.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Botulism alone is incorrect because botulism causes flaccid paralysis, the opposite clinical picture of spastic rigidity seen in tetanus/strychnine.
  • Tetanus alone omits that strychnine poisoning also independently produces the described sawhorse stance with rigidity.
  • Strychnine poisoning alone omits that the sardonic grin and rigid sawhorse stance are also core features of tetanus.
Know More
  • Tetanus toxin blocks glycine release, while strychnine blocks the inhibitory actions of glycine at its receptor directly.
  • Botulism instead causes flaccid paralysis by preventing acetylcholine exocytosis at cholinergic nerve endings.
  • Barbiturates are used to control convulsions in strychnine poisoning.
  • Cats with tetanus may show a characteristic 'pump-handle tail'.

posts.post_title: Which mycotoxin group is specifically associ…
posts.post_content: Which group of mycotoxins is specifically noted as causing reproductive damage, particularly in swine?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Zearalenone, zearalenol and T-2 toxin

Mycotoxins causing reproductive damage are grouped as zearalenone, zearalenol and T-2 toxin.

Correct Option Explanation

Zearalenone acts as a weak oestrogen, inhibiting follicle-stimulating hormone and preovulatory follicle maturation; swine are more susceptible, and cattle exposed develop infertility, nymphomania, anoestrus and vaginitis.

  • Aflatoxins and sterigmatocystin are grouped as mycotoxins that affect the liver, not primarily reproduction.
  • Ochratoxins and citrinin are grouped as mycotoxins that affect the kidneys.
  • Fumonisins, citreoviridin and patulin are grouped as mycotoxins causing neurological effects, not reproductive damage.
Know More
  • Ergot alkaloids are the mycotoxin group producing circulatory disturbances.
  • Rubratoxin, sporodesmin and penicillic acid are additional members of the liver-affecting mycotoxin group.
  • Zearalenone is metabolised to alpha and beta zearalenol and undergoes enterohepatic recycling.
  • Common substrates for zearalenone include corn, wheat, barley and milo.

posts.post_title: Which category of mycotoxins affects the kid…
posts.post_content: Ochratoxins and citrinin are grouped among mycotoxins primarily affecting which organ?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kidneys

Ochratoxins and citrinin are grouped among mycotoxins that primarily affect the kidneys.

Correct Option Explanation

Ochratoxin A is considered the most toxic and common of the ochratoxins, contaminating cereals and grains including barley, sorghum and especially wheat, with demonstrated toxicity in swine, ducklings, chickens, turkeys and dogs.

  • The liver-affecting mycotoxin group instead includes aflatoxins, sterigmatocystin, rubratoxin, sporodesmin and penicillic acid, not ochratoxins.
  • The neurological-effect mycotoxin group instead includes fumonisins, salframin, citreoviridin and patulin.
  • The reproductive-damage mycotoxin group instead includes zearalenone, zearalenol and T-2 toxin.
Know More
  • Ochratoxins comprise at least seven related metabolites (A, B, C, D and their esters) isolated from Aspergillus and Penicillium moulds.
  • Citreoviridin, a Penicillium mycotoxin found in rice, can cause ascending paralysis with respiratory arrest.
  • Patulin is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase, produced by Penicillium and Aspergillus species.
  • Penicillic acid was the first known mycotoxin, implicated in hepatic cirrhosis in swine.

posts.post_title: The clinical syndrome caused by S. aureus an…
posts.post_content: The illness caused by ingestion of discarded, bacterially contaminated foodstuffs (garbage intoxication), commonly due to S. aureus and B. cereus, is best characterized clinically by

_aimcq_options.text: Vomiting followed by diarrhoea, with risk of fluid and electrolyte abnormalities
Sudden death without prior clinical signs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vomiting followed by diarrhoea, with risk of fluid and electrolyte abnormalities

Garbage intoxication typically presents with vomiting (usually within 2-3 hours) followed by diarrhoea within 2-48 hours, risking significant fluid and electrolyte abnormalities.

Correct Option Explanation

Vomiting is often sufficient to remove enough contaminated food to prevent more severe signs, but protracted vomiting and diarrhoea together can quickly cause profound dehydration; treatment focuses on correcting fluid and acid-base imbalances.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Progressive muscle paralysis describes botulism, not the S. aureus/B. cereus enterotoxin syndrome.
  • Cutaneous photosensitization is unrelated to bacterial enterotoxin poisoning; it is a distinct dermatological toxicological phenomenon.
  • The syndrome is characterised by clear preceding gastrointestinal signs, not sudden unexplained death.
Know More
  • S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus that does not form spores, so it can be controlled with proper heat treatment.
  • B. cereus causes a diarrheal illness from heat-labile proteins and an emetic illness from the heat-stable peptide cereulide.
  • Antibiotics are not indicated in uncomplicated cases of garbage intoxication.
  • Activated charcoal should not be given to dehydrated animals unless fluid therapy is also initiated.

posts.post_title: Which spider bite type produces hemolytic an…
posts.post_content: Of the two clinical forms of brown recluse spider bite, which is characterised by hemolytic anaemia, hemoglobinuria, icterus and hyperthermia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Viscerocutaneous form

The viscerocutaneous form of brown recluse spider bite is severe, producing haemolytic anaemia, haemoglobinuria, icterus and hyperthermia.

An unidentified venom component is cytotoxic to endothelial cells, triggering intravascular coagulation and microthrombi formation within capillaries, leading to capillary occlusion, haemorrhage and necrosis.

  • The cutaneous form instead begins as oedema and progresses to an ulcerated wound, without the systemic haemolytic features.
  • A distinct 'neurotoxic form' is not the terminology used for brown recluse bite classification; that description better fits black widow venom effects on nerve calcium transmission.
  • A distinct 'cardiotoxic form' is not among the two forms described for brown recluse spider bite.
Know More
  • About 90% of brown recluse bite cases heal in 1-3 weeks; some may need skin grafting.
  • Black widow spider venom is made up of large proteins affecting calcium ion transmission in nerve cells.
  • Steroids may be used to protect against systemic effects of brown recluse envenomation.
  • Fluids and bicarbonate help minimise haemoglobin deposition in renal tubules in severe haemolytic anaemia.

posts.post_title: Toad venom's cardiac glycoside-like effects…
posts.post_content: Among the compounds found in Bufo toad venom, which components are described as producing digitalis-like cardiac glycoside effects, often resulting in ventricular fibrillation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bufagins and bufotoxins

Bufagins and bufotoxins (conjugated bufagins) have digitalis-like action, often resulting in ventricular fibrillation.

Toad venom contains several components with distinct effects: the cardiac glycoside-like action of bufagins, the pressor effects of catecholamines, and the hallucinogenic effects of indolealkylamines like bufotenins.

  • Catecholamines in toad venom instead produce pressor (blood pressure raising) effects, not the digitalis-like cardiac action.

Know More
  • Bufotenins have oxytocic action and often a marked pressor action, contributing to a third distinct effect of toad venom.
  • Atropine may reduce salivation and the risk of aspiration in toad toxicosis.
  • Thiamylal and halothane anaesthesia may be contraindicated in toad toxicosis due to predisposition to ventricular fibrillation.
  • Tachyarrhythmias in toad toxicosis are treated with lidocaine, phenytoin, propranolol or procainamide.

posts.post_title: The characteristic 'bighead' syndrome with p…
posts.post_content: 'Bighead', characterised by swelling of the ears and head with signs of photosensitivity, high mortality in young animals, is characteristically associated with which plant in sheep?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tribulus terrestris

Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine) causes 'bighead' with swelling of the ears and head, and other signs of photosensitivity in sheep.

Correct Option Explanation

Spiny burs in the plant cause mechanical damage, and toxin levels in the leaves are high from the preflowering to fruiting stages, with high mortality observed among young animals and intensely yellow fat noted throughout the body.

  • Lantana camara causes photosensitization with prominent jaundice and hepatotoxicity/cholestasis, a related but distinct clinical picture involving different toxic principles (lantadenes).

posts.post_title: The primary toxic principle of Parthenium ca…
posts.post_content: Contact with Parthenium, an aggressive invasive weed, causes dermatitis in cattle due to the presence of which toxin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parthenin

Contact with Parthenium causes dermatitis due to the presence of the toxin parthenin, a sesquiterpene lactone.

  • Lantadene is the toxic principle of Lantana camara, not Parthenium.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements correctly…
posts.post_content: Alphanaphthyl thiourea (ANTU), a rodenticide, primarily produces toxicity through which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Increased pulmonary capillary permeability causing pulmonary oedema and hydrothorax
Anticoagulant effect via vitamin K antagonism

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increased pulmonary capillary permeability causing pulmonary oedema and hydrothorax

ANTU increases the permeability of lung capillaries, producing marked hydrothorax and pulmonary oedema.

Correct Option Explanation

The animal effectively 'drowns in its own fluids'; reaction of ANTU with sulphydryl groups may be a necessary part of the mechanism, since sulphydryl-group-blocking agents are effective antidotes in some experimental conditions in rats.

  • Bone marrow suppression describes the cattle-specific toxic mechanism of bracken fern, not ANTU.
  • Hypercalcaemia and soft tissue mineralisation describe cholecalciferol rodenticide toxicity, not ANTU.

posts.post_title: The classical postmortem finding of 'chocola…
posts.post_content: Postmortem blood that appears chocolate brown and clots poorly is a classical finding in which type of poisoning?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nitrate/nitrite poisoning

Chocolate brown coloured blood that clots improperly is a classical postmortem finding of nitrite poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

This colour reflects the presence of methaemoglobin, formed when nitrite oxidises the ferrous iron of haemoglobin to the ferric state, which cannot carry oxygen, producing the discoloured, poorly clotting blood.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Arsenic poisoning is instead associated with gastroenteritis and haemorrhage without the characteristic chocolate-brown blood colour change.
  • Lead poisoning shows no characteristic gross blood colour change; basophilic stippling is a microscopic finding, not a gross colour change.
  • Fluoride poisoning primarily affects teeth and bone rather than producing a characteristic blood colour change.
Know More
  • In carbon monoxide poisoning, blood is instead characteristically cherry red.
  • Methylene blue given intravenously (4-8 mg/kg) is used to treat nitrite-induced methaemoglobinaemia.
  • Toxic symptoms of nitrite poisoning appear once 20% of haemoglobin is converted to methaemoglobin.

posts.post_title: Which species is noted to be uniquely resist…

posts.post_title: The characteristic 'mad dog running' clinica…

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

'Mad dog running' — aimless running, howling and teeth snapping — is a documented clinical sign in dogs affected by zinc phosphide poisoning.

posts.post_title: Which of the following best captures the def…
posts.post_content: Which statement best defines toxicology as a scientific discipline?

_aimcq_options.text: Toxicology is exclusively the legal study of poisoning deaths
Toxicology is the study of the adverse effects of chemical, physical or biological agents on living organisms and the ecosystem
Toxicology is limited to the study of pesticide residues in food

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Toxicology is the study of the adverse effects of chemical, physical or biological agents on living organisms and the ecosystem

Toxicology is the science of the adverse effects of chemical, physical or biological agents on living organisms and the ecosystem, including the prevention and amelioration of such effects.

Correct Option Explanation

Toxicology is studied under three interconnected phases: the exposure phase, the toxicokinetic phase (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and the toxicodynamic phase (interaction with target tissue producing toxic effects).

Incorrect Options Analysis

Know More
  • The word 'toxic' is derived from the Greek word 'toxikon', originally referring to arrow poison.
  • Veterinary toxicology deals specifically with the harmful effects of chemicals on domestic animals, wildlife and, through food-producing animals, on human health.
  • Other branches include clinical toxicology, forensic toxicology, industrial toxicology, environmental toxicology, economic toxicology and regulatory toxicology.
  • Toxicokinetics studies absorption, distribution, biotransformation and excretion of the toxic agent within the body.

posts.post_title: Which term describes exposure to two or more…

Correct Answer: Synergistic (potentiating) effect

A combined effect greater than the sum of individual effects of two or more toxicants is a synergistic or potentiating effect.

This is an important chemical-related factor modifying toxicity: certain combinations of drugs or toxicants can enhance one another's toxic action well beyond what either would cause alone, complicating diagnosis and treatment of mixed exposures.

posts.post_title: Which of the following best describes the me…

_aimcq_options.text: Adsorbing the toxicant onto its surface, reducing systemic absorption

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Activated charcoal works by adsorbing the toxicant onto its large surface area within the gastrointestinal tract, thereby reducing its systemic absorption.

posts.post_title: Which statement about the role of the liver…
posts.post_content: Regarding the liver's role in handling absorbed toxicants, which of the following statements is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: The liver has no role in detoxification of xenobiotics
The liver is the major site of biotransformation but its metabolites are always less toxic than the parent compound

The liver only stores toxicants without any metabolic modification

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The liver is the major site of biotransformation, though some metabolites can be more toxic than the parent compound (lethal synthesis)

The liver is the major site of biotransformation, but not all metabolism is protective — some pathways create more toxic metabolites, a process termed lethal synthesis.

Correct Option Explanation

Classic examples are parathion, converted to the more toxic paraoxon, and fluoroacetate, converted to toxic fluorocitrate; biotransformation occurs through phase I (oxidation, hydroxylation, deamination, dealkylation) and phase II (conjugation) reactions.

  • Cats have poorly developed glucuronic acid conjugating capacity, a key phase II pathway.
  • Swine have low sulfotransferase activity, limiting sulfate conjugation.

Highly protein-bound toxicants remain largely confined to the vascular compartment and are poorly cleared by dialysis techniques that rely on diffusion of the free (unbound) fraction across the peritoneal membrane.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about tole…

posts.post_title: Which statement correctly describes the trea…
posts.post_content: In treating oxalate poisoning, calcium salts such as calcium gluconate or calcium borogluconate are administered mainly to

posts.post_title: In sheep, molybdenum toxicity is treated by…
posts.post_content: Chronic molybdenum toxicity (teart) in cattle and sheep is treated by daily administration of which compound?

posts.post_title: The antidote ammonium tetrathiomolybdate is…

  • The chronicity factor (ratio of acute to chronic LD50) greater than 2.0 indicates a relatively cumulative toxicant.
  • Sub-acute toxicity studies typically administer low doses for 90 days to determine the NOEL.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is correctly identifi…
posts.post_content: Which of the following organophosphate compounds is classified as directly acting, not requiring metabolic activation for its anticholinesterase toxicity?

TEPP (tetraethyl pyrophosphate) is classified as a directly acting organophosphate, not requiring metabolic activation.

Correct Option Explanation

TEPP was the first organophosphate introduced during World War II; other directly acting compounds include DFP, tabun, sarin, soman and diazinon, all of which exert cholinesterase inhibition without needing prior metabolic conversion.

  • High temperature increases parathion toxicity while low temperature increases malathion toxicity in mice.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about carb…
posts.post_content: Carbaryl (Sevin), described as the best known carbamate insecticide, additionally inhibits which enzyme in insects besides acetylcholinesterase?

Carbamates, including carbaryl, additionally inhibit the aliesterase enzyme in insects, beyond their main action on acetylcholinesterase.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding metabolites of organochlorine pesticides like DDT, which of the following is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Metabolites such as dieldrin and heptachlor epoxide are rapidly degraded and non-persistent
Metabolites such as dieldrin and heptachlor epoxide are persistent both in the body and the environment

Organochlorines do not form any metabolites

Organochlorine metabolites like dieldrin and heptachlor epoxide are persistent both in the body and in the environment.

This persistence, combined with high lipid solubility of the parent compounds, favours bioaccumulation and biomagnification up food chains, a defining toxicological characteristic of the organochlorine pesticide class heavily used from 1950 to the 1970s.

  • Lindane toxicosis is common in cats and dogs though never approved for use in cats.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements correctly…
posts.post_content: The characteristic rotting-fish odour of liberated phosphine gas is a shared feature useful in diagnosing poisoning by which two related rodenticide/fumigant compounds?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Zinc phosphide and aluminium phosphide

Both zinc phosphide and aluminium phosphide liberate phosphine gas with a characteristic rotting fish odour, aiding diagnosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Phosphine gas blocks cytochrome oxidase, reducing energy production and increasing reactive oxygen species; aluminium phosphide's phosphine, being heavier than air, sinks through stored grain rather than rising and polluting the atmosphere.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Anticoagulant rodenticides and bromethalin act via entirely different mechanisms (vitamin K antagonism and Na-K ATPase disruption respectively) and do not share this phosphine odour clue.
  • Metaldehyde is instead associated with an acetaldehyde odour, and strychnine has no characteristic diagnostic odour described.
  • Cholecalciferol and warfarin act via hypercalcaemia and vitamin K antagonism respectively, neither producing the phosphine odour.
Know More
  • Zinc phosphide poisoning in dogs shows the characteristic 'mad dog running' behaviour — aimless running, howling and teeth snapping.
  • Sodium bicarbonate can be given to reduce conversion of zinc phosphide to phosphine gas in the stomach.
  • Aluminium phosphide is applied to stored grain as sachets or tablets that react with moisture to release phosphine.
  • Both compounds cause pulmonary oedema, ventricular arrhythmias and kidney damage in poisoned animals.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements correctly…
posts.post_content: Sodium bicarbonate administration in zinc phosphide poisoning serves to

Know More
  • Zinc phosphide poisoning produces the characteristic 'mad dog running' behaviour in affected dogs.
  • Phosphine gas has an odour resembling rotting fish, shared with aluminium phosphide exposure.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about Fusa…
posts.post_content: Fusarium moniliforme, notably associated with corn, is the source of which mycotoxin group?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fumonisins

Fusarium moniliforme is the source of fumonisins, particularly fumonisin B1, primarily contaminating corn.

Correct Option Explanation

Fumonisin B1 inhibits sphingosine N-acyltransferase, disrupting sphingolipid metabolism; in horses this causes equine leukoencephalomalacia (ELEM), historically called moldy corn poisoning, with signs including depression, ataxia, blindness and hysteria.

  • Ochratoxins are produced by different Aspergillus and Penicillium species, unrelated to Fusarium moniliforme.

  • Swine exposed to fumonisin develop pulmonary oedema and liver disease rather than the neurotoxic syndrome seen in horses.

  • Characteristic liquefactive necrosis of white matter in the brain may only be evident histologically even in fatal equine cases.
  • Climatic conditions predisposing to fumonisin contamination include midsummer drought and an early wet fall.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements correctly…
posts.post_content: Claviceps purpurea, the fungus responsible for ergotism, produces which class of toxic compounds causing circulatory disturbances?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ergot alkaloids

Claviceps purpurea produces ergot alkaloids, causing circulatory disturbances historically known as ergotism or 'holy fire'.

Correct Option Explanation

Ergot alkaloids cause vasoconstriction leading to gangrenous extremities; more than 40,000 people died of ergotism in France and Spain in 992, and the syndrome was later also called St. Antony's fire.

  • Fumonisins are instead produced by Fusarium moniliforme, causing neurological syndromes rather than the vascular effects of ergotism.
  • Zearalenone is produced by Fusarium roseum and causes reproductive damage, unrelated to circulatory disturbances.
  • Aflatoxins are produced by Aspergillus species, primarily affecting the liver, not the circulatory system in the manner of ergot alkaloids.
Know More
  • Rubratoxin, sporodesmin and penicillic acid are additional members of the mycotoxin group affecting the liver.
  • Penicillic acid was the first known mycotoxin, implicated in hepatic cirrhosis in swine.
  • Ergotism's 'holy' descriptor reflected beliefs it was divine punishment, while 'fire' referred to the burning sensation in affected extremities.
  • Ergot contamination of rye and other grains was historically a major cause of epidemic poisoning in medieval Europe.

posts.post_title: Which of the following correctly describes c…
posts.post_content: Citreoviridin, a Penicillium mycotoxin found in rice, is documented to cause which effect?

Citreoviridin, a Penicillium mycotoxin found in rice, can cause ascending paralysis with respiratory arrest.

  • Patulin, another Penicillium/Aspergillus mycotoxin, is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase.
  • Fumonisin B1 causes equine leukoencephalomalacia (ELEM), a related but distinct neurological mycotoxicosis in horses.

  • Zearalenone, zearalenol and T-2 toxin are grouped as mycotoxins causing reproductive damage.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about tann…
posts.post_content: In hemlock (Conium maculatum) poisoning, tannic acid is administered as part of treatment because it

  • Reversing acetylcholinesterase phosphorylation is the role of oximes like pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning, not tannic acid in hemlock poisoning.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding the two broad causes of photosensitization, which of the following is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Primary photosensitization involves absorption of a photodynamic agent unchanged from skin or gut; secondary involves impaired hepatobiliary excretion of phylloerythrin
Primary and secondary photosensitization are caused by identical mechanisms
Secondary photosensitization always occurs without any liver involvement
Primary photosensitization is always caused by phylloerythrin accumulation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Primary photosensitization involves absorption of a photodynamic agent unchanged from skin or gut; secondary involves impaired hepatobiliary excretion of phylloerythrin

Primary photosensitization involves absorption of an agent (e.g. hypericin) unchanged from skin or gut; secondary (hepatogenous) photosensitization results from impaired hepatobiliary excretion of phylloerythrin.

Correct Option Explanation

Secondary photosensitization is by far the most frequent type seen in livestock, and phylloerythrin is derived from chlorophyll breakdown by gastrointestinal microorganisms, normally excreted efficiently in bile until hepatic dysfunction intervenes.

  • The two mechanisms are explicitly distinct — primary involves an unmetabolised agent while secondary specifically involves hepatobiliary dysfunction.

  • Tribulus terrestris and Lantana camara are plants implicated in phylloerythrin-mediated (secondary) photosensitization.
  • Type II photosensitivity (aberrant pigment synthesis) is a third distinct category, e.g. bovine erythropoietic protoporphyria.
  • Type IV photosensitivity has an unknown pathogenesis, e.g. with Kochia scoparia.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements correctly…
posts.post_content: Lantana camara toxicity, mediated by pentacyclic triterpene acids including lantadenes A-D and icterogenin, primarily produces which effect?

_aimcq_options.text: Cholestasis and hepatotoxicity with prominent jaundice
Hypercalcaemia from excess vitamin D activity

Lantana camara toxicity, mediated by lantadenes A-D and icterogenin, produces cholestasis and hepatotoxicity with prominent jaundice.

Correct Option Explanation

  • Direct acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates/carbamates, not lantadenes.
  • Hypercalcaemia from vitamin D activity is the mechanism of cholecalciferol rodenticide toxicity, unrelated to Lantana camara.

  • Secondary (hepatogenous) photosensitization is the most common type observed in livestock generally.

  • Corticosteroids given parenterally in early stages may help manage photosensitization.

posts.post_content: Regarding acetaminophen toxicity, which statement correctly describes the role of hepatic glutathione?

Glutathione has no relevance to acetaminophen metabolism
N-acetylcysteine depletes remaining glutathione, worsening toxicity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Glutathione depletion allows the reactive metabolite to bind hepatocyte constituents, causing necrosis

Depletion of hepatic glutathione stores allows the reactive electrophilic metabolite of acetaminophen to bind hepatocyte constituents, causing hepatic necrosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Acetaminophen is metabolised by cytochrome P450 into this reactive metabolite; N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione surrogate, replenishing depleted stores, and is most effective if given within 8-16 hours of ingestion.

  • It is depletion, not excess, of glutathione that permits the toxic metabolite to accumulate and cause damage.

  • Glucagon is a physiologic antagonist effective even during profound beta-blockade.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about oral…
posts.post_content: Regarding ricin toxicity from Ricinus communis (castor bean), which of the following is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Ricin is equally toxic by all routes of administration
Ricin is approximately 100 times less toxic orally than parenterally
Ricin is more toxic orally than parenterally
Ricin has no toxicity by any route

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ricin is approximately 100 times less toxic orally than parenterally

Ricin is orally 100 times less toxic than parenterally.

Correct Option Explanation

This large difference reflects poor and variable gastrointestinal absorption of the protein toxin compared with direct parenteral exposure; ricin is a heat-labile protein and is generally inactivated by heating during processing of castor bean cake or meal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ricin's toxicity clearly does vary substantially by route, contrary to a claim of equal toxicity across all routes.
  • Ricin is in fact less, not more, toxic orally compared with the parenteral route.
  • Ricin is a well-documented potent toxalbumin with significant toxicity by multiple routes, contrary to a claim of no toxicity.

  • Ricin acts as a proteolytic enzyme with strong inhibitory effects on ribosomal protein synthesis.
  • Ricinine, another castor bean phytotoxin, is reportedly goitrogenic.
  • Ascorbic acid administration is reported to increase survival rates in ricin toxicosis.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about abri…
posts.post_content: Regarding abrin, the toxin from Abrus precatorius, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Abrin is fully degraded by gastric juices before it can act
Abrin can be selectively transported by neurons, a phenomenon called suicidal transport
Abrin has no effect on ribosomal protein synthesis
Abrin is safe to implant subcutaneously in cattle

Correct Answer: Abrin can be selectively transported by neurons, a phenomenon called suicidal transport

Abrin's peculiar binding potential allows it to be selectively transported by neurons, called suicidal transport.

Abrin is neither degraded nor altered by gastric juices, allowing it to remain active; it is an important cytotoxin that inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis and causes RBC agglutination, similar in some respects to ricin.

  • Abrin can also act as an antigen, and protective antibodies may be elicited against it.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Presence of ferrous sulphate in the diet is recommended when feeding cottonseed products because it helps prevent toxicity from which compound?

Presence of ferrous sulphate in the diet prevents gossypol toxicity from cottonseed.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about brac…
posts.post_content: Bracken fern-induced bovine enzootic haematuria in cattle is at least partly attributable to which suspected carcinogen?

Bovine enzootic haematuria caused by bracken fern is at least partly attributable to the suspected carcinogen ptaquiloside.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Which of the following correctly places diphacinone and chlorophacinone within the anticoagulant rodenticide generational classification?

_aimcq_options.text: First-generation, requiring multiple feedings like warfarin
Intermediate anticoagulants, requiring fewer feedings than first-generation agents
Second-generation, toxic after a single feeding
Not anticoagulants at all, but neurotoxic rodenticides

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Dicobalt edetate is used as a specific antidote in which type of poisoning?

Correct Answer: Cyanide poisoning

Dicobalt edetate forms stable non-toxic complexes with cyanide, serving as a specific antidote.

  • Fluorocitrate, from sodium fluoroacetate metabolism, similarly blocks the citric acid cycle by inhibiting aconitase, a related but distinct mechanism.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Desferrioxamine forms a stable complex specifically with which metal, giving urine a reddish (vin rose) colour upon excretion?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ferric iron

Desferrioxamine is specific for iron, forming a stable complex with ferric iron that is excreted, giving urine a reddish (vin rose) colour.

Correct Option Explanation

  • Penicillamine, a metabolite of penicillin, is used to chelate both lead and copper.
  • Sodium calcium edetate works specifically by exchanging calcium for lead, with the lead chelate excreted in urine.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Copper acetoarsenite (Paris green) was historically used for which purpose?

_aimcq_options.text: As a chelating antidote for lead poisoning

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: As an insecticide
