posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Which of the following correctly matches a toxin category with its biological source?

_aimcq_options.text: Mycotoxins are produced by fungi/moulds; phytotoxins are produced by plants
Mycotoxins are produced by plants; phytotoxins are produced by fungi
Zootoxins are produced by fungi; mycotoxins are produced by animals
All toxin categories share an identical biological source

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mycotoxins are produced by fungi/moulds; phytotoxins are produced by plants

Mycotoxins are toxins produced by fungi/moulds; phytotoxins are toxins produced by plants.

Correct Option Explanation

This is part of the broader classification of biologically-derived toxins, which also includes zootoxins (from lower animals via bite/sting, also called venoms) and bacterial toxins (endotoxins and exotoxins).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This option reverses the actual source relationship — mycotoxins come from fungi, and phytotoxins come from plants, not the other way around.
  • Zootoxins actually come from animals (via bite or sting), and mycotoxins come from fungi, the reverse of what this option states.
  • Each toxin category clearly has a distinct biological source, not an identical one, as the terminology itself demonstrates.
Know More
  • Toxinology is the study of the toxic effects of toxins of biological origin.
  • Toxicosis is the general condition resulting from exposure to poisons, used interchangeably with poisoning and intoxication.
  • Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharide complexes on Gram-negative bacterial outer membranes.
  • Botulinum and tetanus toxins are classic examples of potent bacterial exotoxins.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding the primary factor affecting absorption of a toxicant from any exposure route, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Solubility is the primary factor affecting absorption
Colour of the compound is the primary factor affecting absorption
Only molecular weight determines absorption, regardless of solubility
Absorption is entirely independent of a compound's physical properties

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Solubility is the primary factor affecting absorption

Solubility is the primary factor affecting absorption of a toxicant.

Correct Option Explanation

This principle applies broadly: soluble arsenic salts are more toxic than insoluble ones, soluble lead salts like lead acetate are more toxic than insoluble lead oxide, and insoluble/ionised compounds are generally poorly absorbed through intact skin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Colour is not identified as a factor affecting absorption in the source material; it is unrelated to a compound's physicochemical absorption behaviour.
  • Molecular weight alone is not described as the primary determinant; solubility is specifically named as the key factor.
  • Absorption is explicitly dependent on physical/chemical properties like solubility, contrary to a claim of complete independence.
Know More
  • Inhalation and intravenous routes generally produce the fastest, most intense toxic effects due to bypassing absorption barriers.
  • Presence of feed in the stomach can dilute toxins and delay intoxication, an effect greater in ruminants.
  • DMSO increases the rate and degree of cutaneous absorption of xenobiotics applied concurrently.
  • Constipation increases toxicity while diarrhoea decreases absorption of ingested poisons.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Among domestic species, which of the following is correctly identified as relatively resistant to lead poisoning?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Goats, swine and chicken

Goats, swine and chicken are relatively resistant to lead poisoning among domestic species.

Correct Option Explanation

This species-level difference in susceptibility contrasts with pregnant ewes, who are specifically noted as more susceptible to lead poisoning, illustrating that both species and physiological state (pregnancy) influence overall vulnerability.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pregnant ewes are specifically noted as more susceptible, not relatively resistant, to lead poisoning.
  • Cattle in general are not specifically identified as the resistant group; the resistant group named is goats, swine and chicken.
  • Dogs are not specifically named among the resistant species; lead poisoning in dogs is well documented with characteristic signs like basophilic stippling and nervous signs.
Know More
  • Sheep may acquire a taste for lead and preferentially graze high-contamination areas, increasing their risk.
  • Rate of ingestion matters: large amounts ingested over one or two days are more toxic than the same total dose spread out.
  • About 95% of the body burden of absorbed lead is found in bone, the 'bone sink for lead'.
  • Basophilic stippling of red cells and nucleated RBCs are associated with lead poisoning specifically in dogs.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Datura stramonium produces toxic effects mainly through which category of alkaloids?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tropane (belladonna-type) alkaloids with parasympatholytic action

Datura stramonium contains tropane (belladonna-type) alkaloids that produce parasympatholytic effects, similar to Atropa belladonna.

Correct Option Explanation

These alkaloids competitively block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, producing signs such as mydriasis (pupil dilation), dry mouth, tachycardia and CNS excitement, distinguishing this plant's toxic mechanism from cardiac glycoside or thiaminase-based plant toxins.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cardiac glycosides similar to oleander are instead the toxic principle of Nerium oleander, a chemically and mechanistically distinct plant toxin from Datura's tropane alkaloids.
  • A thiaminase enzyme mechanism is instead relevant to bracken fern toxicity in horses, unrelated to Datura.
  • n-Propyl disulphide is the toxic principle of Allium species (onion/garlic), an entirely different plant toxin from Datura's alkaloids.
Know More
  • Rabbits possess the enzyme atropinase, conferring relative resistance to atropine and related tropane alkaloids like those in Datura.
  • Atropa belladonna shares the same broad category of tropane alkaloids as Datura.
  • Conium maculatum (hemlock) contains the distinct alkaloid coniine, unrelated chemically to tropane alkaloids.
  • Datura seeds are a common cause of accidental poisoning when mixed with grain or forage.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding species differences in sodium fluoroacetate (Compound 1080) toxicity, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Primates and birds are resistant, while carnivores are more susceptible
Birds are the most susceptible species while carnivores are fully resistant
All vertebrate species show identical susceptibility
Susceptibility to sodium fluoroacetate has never been characterised across species

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Primates and birds are resistant, while carnivores are more susceptible

Primates and birds are relatively resistant to sodium fluoroacetate, while carnivores are more susceptible.

Correct Option Explanation

This species difference is clinically relevant: CNS stimulation predominates in dogs (a carnivore) while cardiac effects predominate in horses, sheep, goats and chickens after fluoroacetate is converted to fluorocitrate, which inhibits aconitase and blocks the tricarboxylic acid cycle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • This option reverses the documented relationship — birds are relatively resistant, and carnivores are susceptible, not the other way around.
  • Species clearly show different, not identical, susceptibility to sodium fluoroacetate, as reflected in the documented primate/bird resistance versus carnivore susceptibility.
  • Species susceptibility to sodium fluoroacetate is in fact well characterised, contrary to a claim that it has never been studied.
Know More
  • There is a characteristic lag phase of at least 30 minutes before clinical signs of fluoroacetate poisoning begin.
  • No specific antidotal treatment is available for sodium fluoroacetate poisoning.
  • Fluoroacetate poisoning causes energy depletion, lactate/citrate accumulation and decreased blood pH.
  • Thallium, another cellular poison, is instead treated with diphenylthiocarbazone and Prussian blue.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Prussian blue is administered in thallium poisoning primarily to

_aimcq_options.text: Directly chelate lead in the bloodstream

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Prevent enterohepatic recycling of thallium

Prussian blue is given in thallium poisoning to prevent enterohepatic recycling of the metal.

Correct Option Explanation

Thallium is a cellular poison acting via inhibition of sulphur-containing compounds; diphenylthiocarbazone is also antidotal if given within 24 hours, working alongside Prussian blue's action of interrupting the enterohepatic cycle to reduce ongoing reabsorption.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Prussian blue is not a lead chelator; that role in lead poisoning belongs to sodium calcium edetate and dimercaprol (BAL).
  • Reactivating phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase is the role of oximes like pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning, unrelated to thallium treatment.
  • Correcting hypocalcaemia from oxalate binding is relevant to oxalate plant poisoning, an entirely different toxicant from thallium.
Know More
  • Diphenylthiocarbazone is antidotal for thallium poisoning specifically if given within 24 hours of exposure.
  • Thallium's mechanism involves inhibition of sulphur-containing compounds at the cellular level.
  • Sodium fluoroacetate, by contrast, has no specific antidotal treatment available.
  • Fluorocitrate, formed from sodium fluoroacetate, inhibits aconitase and blocks the tricarboxylic acid cycle.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: The type II ('CS') pyrethroid syndrome, associated with alpha-cyano compounds, is characterised by

_aimcq_options.text: Only mild local skin irritation with no systemic signs
Exclusive cardiac arrhythmia with no neurologic involvement

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Salivation, choreoathetosis and paresthesia

The type II ('CS') pyrethroid syndrome, from alpha-cyano compounds, is characterised by salivation, choreoathetosis and paresthesia.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with the type I ('T') syndrome of increased sensitivity to stimuli and whole-body tremor seen with compounds like allethrin and permethrin, reflecting the structural distinction conferred by the alpha-cyano moiety present in deltamethrin, cypermethrin, fenvalerate, fluvalinate and flumethrin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The type II syndrome produces significant systemic neurologic signs, not merely mild local skin irritation without systemic involvement.
  • Hypercalcaemia and soft tissue mineralisation describe cholecalciferol rodenticide toxicity, an entirely unrelated toxicant class from pyrethroids.
  • The syndrome involves prominent neurologic signs (salivation, choreoathetosis, paresthesia) alongside any cardiac effects, not exclusive cardiac involvement without neurologic signs.
Know More
  • Cats with severe tremors from concentrated permethrin exposure often improve after IV methocarbamol.
  • Pyrethroids act on sodium ion channels, decreasing peak sodium conductance and suppressing potassium conduction.
  • Phenothiazine tranquilizers are contraindicated in treating pyrethroid toxicosis seizures.
  • Type I pyrethroids include allethrin, permethrin and cismethrin.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Which of the following correctly matches a toxicant with the tissue in which it is selectively deposited?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Arsenic - hair and nails

Arsenic is correctly matched with selective deposition in hair and nails.

Correct Option Explanation

Once deposited in keratinised hair cells, arsenic is irremovable and moves slowly along the hair as it grows, making hair analysis a valuable tool for detecting chronic arsenic exposure over time.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mercury compounds (mercurials) are instead selectively deposited in the kidneys, not the thyroid.
  • Iodine is instead selectively deposited in the thyroid, not the skeleton.
  • Lead, along with fluorine and strontium, is instead selectively deposited in the skeleton (bone), not the lungs — paraquat is the agent selectively deposited in lungs.
Know More
  • Halogenated hydrocarbons are selectively deposited in adipose tissue.
  • Primaquine is selectively deposited in the liver.
  • Selective tissue affinity does not necessarily indicate pathological lesions will develop at that site, but is important for toxicological analysis.
  • Hair samples (5-10 g) are useful for detecting dermal pesticide exposure and chronic accumulation of arsenic or selenium.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding the copper-to-molybdenum ratio in ruminant diets, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: A chronic excessive copper-to-molybdenum ratio predisposes to acute copper poisoning
A chronic excessive copper-to-molybdenum ratio has no effect on copper toxicity risk
Only molybdenum deficiency alone causes copper poisoning, regardless of copper intake
Increasing molybdenum always increases the risk of copper toxicity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A chronic excessive copper-to-molybdenum ratio predisposes to acute copper poisoning

Copper toxicity most seriously arises as an acute syndrome linked to a chronic excessive copper-to-molybdenum dietary ratio.

Correct Option Explanation

Sheep are especially prone to copper poisoning, particularly with molybdenum deficiency in the diet, since molybdenum (along with sulphate) normally helps limit hepatic copper accumulation; when this ratio is skewed toward excess copper, chronic accumulation can trigger an acute haemolytic crisis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The copper-to-molybdenum ratio clearly does have a significant, well-documented effect on copper toxicity risk, contrary to a claim of no effect.
  • Both molybdenum deficiency and elevated copper intake together contribute to the risk, not molybdenum deficiency alone irrespective of copper intake.
  • Increasing molybdenum (with adequate sulphate) actually tends to protect against copper toxicity by limiting hepatic copper accumulation, the opposite of always increasing risk.
Know More
  • Bedlington terriers have a genetic defect causing excessive hepatic copper storage, a separate cause of copper toxicity.
  • Affected animals with copper poisoning void port wine coloured urine due to haemoglobinuria.
  • The bluish-black kidney lesion, 'gun-metal kidney', is characteristic of chronic copper poisoning.
  • Daily administration of copper sulphate, conversely, is used to treat the opposite condition of molybdenum toxicity.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding postmortem findings in acute arsenic poisoning, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Severe gastroenteritis with capillary damage in the gut is a characteristic finding
No gastrointestinal lesions are ever found in arsenic poisoning
Arsenic exclusively causes lesions in the respiratory tract, not the gut
Arsenic poisoning always spares the vascular system entirely

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Severe gastroenteritis with capillary damage in the gut is a characteristic finding

Severe gastroenteritis with capillary damage in the gut is a characteristic postmortem finding of acute arsenic poisoning.

Correct Option Explanation

Arsenic is a potent capillary poison, with splanchnic beds being particularly sensitive, explaining the severe gastrointestinal haemorrhage and damage seen at postmortem examination, consistent with its mechanism of inactivating sulphydryl-dependent enzymes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Gastrointestinal lesions are, in fact, a hallmark, well-documented postmortem finding in arsenic poisoning, not an absent feature.
  • Arsenic's capillary poison effects are specifically emphasised in the splanchnic (gut) vascular beds, not exclusively the respiratory tract.
  • Arsenic clearly does affect the vascular system significantly, as reflected in its description as a potent capillary poison, contrary to a claim of vascular sparing.
Know More
  • Arsenic poisoning is more common in bovines and felines; occasional in dogs, rare in swine and poultry.
  • After absorption, arsenicals accumulate in the liver initially, and with continued exposure, in bone, skin and keratinised tissue.
  • Dimercaprol (BAL) binds arsenic to form a non-toxic arsenic-mercaptide complex that is easily excreted.
  • Sodium thiosulphate can be given both orally and intravenously in arsenic poisoning treatment.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Ethanol or 4-methylpyrazole are used in ethylene glycol poisoning because they

_aimcq_options.text: Compete for alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing formation of toxic acid metabolites
Directly neutralise calcium oxalate crystals already formed in the kidney

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Compete for alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing formation of toxic acid metabolites

Ethanol and 4-methylpyrazole compete for alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing formation of the toxic acid metabolites of ethylene glycol.

Correct Option Explanation

This competitive inhibition strategy prevents the enzyme from converting ethylene glycol into its more toxic downstream metabolites, which would otherwise cause severe metabolic acidosis and renal calcium oxalate crystal deposition.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • These agents do not directly dissolve or neutralise crystals already deposited in the kidney; they act upstream by blocking further toxic metabolite formation.
  • Reactivating phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase is the role of oximes like pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning, unrelated to ethylene glycol treatment.
  • Chelating absorbed lead is the role of agents like sodium calcium edetate, unrelated to ethylene glycol's alcohol dehydrogenase-based treatment mechanism.
Know More
  • Ethylene glycol poisoning produces calcium oxalate crystalluria, a feature it shares mechanistically with plant oxalate poisoning.
  • Calcium salts such as calcium gluconate are used to treat the hypocalcaemia resulting from oxalate binding calcium.
  • N-acetylcysteine, by contrast, is the specific antidote for acetaminophen toxicity, a different mechanism entirely.
  • Blood samples (5-10 ml) are useful for detecting exposure to ethylene glycol among other toxicants.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding diagnostic urine colour clues in poisoning, which statement correctly matches phenothiazine exposure with the resulting urine colour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Red urine - phenothiazine

Red coloured urine is a diagnostic clue associated with phenothiazine exposure.

Correct Option Explanation

This colour change, alongside other urine colour clues, aids clinical diagnosis of specific poisonings: dark green urine follows phenolic compound exposure, while blood colour changes (cherry red for carbon monoxide, chocolate brown for nitrite/chlorate) provide complementary diagnostic information.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dark green urine is instead the documented colour clue for phenolic compound exposure, not phenothiazine.
  • Chocolate brown is instead the documented colour for blood in nitrite/chlorate poisoning, not urine colour in phenothiazine exposure.
  • Phenothiazine exposure specifically produces a documented colour change (red), not colourless urine.
Know More
  • Copper poisoning produces characteristically deep green faeces due to a copper-chlorophyll complex.
  • Cyanide poisoning is associated with a characteristic bitter almond breath odour.
  • Phosphorus poisoning is associated with a characteristic garlic breath and gastrointestinal odour.
  • Hemlock poisoning is associated with a distinctive mouse-like breath and urine odour from excreted coniine.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: In ruminants, in addition to the small and large intestine, which additional gastrointestinal compartments are noted as important absorption sites for ingested toxicants?

_aimcq_options.text: Only the abomasum, never the rumen

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rumen and reticulum

In ruminants, the rumen and reticulum are also important absorption sites for ingested toxicants, in addition to the small intestine.

Correct Option Explanation

This reflects the unique digestive physiology of ruminants, where large volumes of ingesta and prolonged residence time in the forestomachs create additional opportunities for toxicant absorption compared with monogastric species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The omasum and abomasum are not specifically named as the key additional absorption sites in this context; the rumen and reticulum are the ones identified.
  • The oesophagus and mouth are conduits for ingesta transit rather than being identified as significant absorption sites for toxicants.
  • The rumen is explicitly identified as an important absorption site in ruminants, contrary to a claim that it never absorbs toxicants.
Know More
  • The small intestine is the generally important site of absorption, with the large intestine also important in non-ruminants.
  • Presence of feed in the stomach/rumen dilutes toxins and can delay intoxication, an effect greater in ruminants.
  • Rumen microorganisms are responsible for converting nitrate to the more toxic nitrite in nitrate poisoning.
  • Rumen urease hydrolyses urea to liberate ammonia, the toxic agent in urea/NPN poisoning.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Curare and sea snake venoms, with a lethal dose around 0.1 mg/kg, fall into which toxicity classification?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Extremely toxic

Curare and sea snake venoms, with a lethal dose around 0.1 mg/kg, fall into the extremely toxic classification (<1 mg/kg).

Correct Option Explanation

This places them in the most potent toxicity category, even more potent than compounds like strychnine (2 mg/kg, highly toxic) and comparable in order of magnitude to tetrodotoxin (0.01 mg/kg) and botulinum toxins (<0.0001 mg/kg).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Slightly toxic corresponds to a much higher (less potent) lethal dose range of 0.5-5 g/kg, far above 0.1 mg/kg.
  • Practically non-toxic corresponds to 5-15 g/kg, vastly less potent than the 0.1 mg/kg range of curare/sea snake venom.
  • Relatively harmless corresponds to more than 15 g/kg, the least potent classification, far removed from 0.1 mg/kg potency.
Know More
  • Botulinum toxins are lethal at less than 0.0001 mg/kg, among the most potent known toxins.
  • Tetrodotoxin has an acute lethal dose of about 0.01 mg/kg.
  • Compounds classed as highly toxic have a lethal dose of 1-50 mg/kg, e.g. strychnine.
  • A compound is classified as extremely toxic if its lethal dose is less than 1 mg/kg.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding the most common source of botulinum toxin for animals, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Decaying carcasses, often with maggots serving as vectors, are the most common source
Fresh, uncontaminated forage is the primary source
Botulinum toxin is only found in unopened, sterile canned products fed to animals
Botulism has no environmental source and only arises from vaccination

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Decaying carcasses, often with maggots serving as vectors, are the most common source

The most common source of botulinum toxin for animals is decaying carcasses, with maggots often serving as vectors.

Correct Option Explanation

Clostridium botulinum proliferates in decomposing organic material, and animals scavenging or accidentally ingesting contaminated carcass material (or maggots that have fed on it) become exposed to the preformed toxin, which acts as a zinc metalloendoprotease at cholinergic nerve endings.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Fresh, uncontaminated forage is not identified as a botulinum toxin source; decaying organic material is specifically implicated instead.
  • While improperly processed canned goods are a classically recognised source of botulism in some contexts, this option's framing of exclusively sterile canned products is incorrect, and it is not the source specifically named as most common for animals here.
  • Botulism clearly does have a well-documented environmental source (decaying carcasses), contrary to a claim of no environmental source.
Know More
  • Serotype C is most commonly implicated in botulism of dogs, waterfowl and poultry.
  • Serotype B has been a particular problem in horses and cattle.
  • Death from botulism results from respiratory failure due to blocked acetylcholine exocytosis.
  • Carbamylcholine may be used in cattle to stimulate gastrointestinal motility, enhancing toxin removal.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding predisposing dietary factors for copper poisoning in sheep, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Molybdenum deficiency in the diet predisposes sheep to copper poisoning
Excess dietary molybdenum always predisposes to copper poisoning
Sheep are entirely unaffected by dietary copper levels
Only cattle, never sheep, are susceptible to copper poisoning

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Molybdenum deficiency in the diet predisposes sheep to copper poisoning

Sheep are especially prone to copper poisoning, particularly with molybdenum deficiency in the diet.

Correct Option Explanation

Molybdenum (together with sulphate) normally helps limit hepatic copper storage; when dietary molybdenum is deficient, copper accumulates progressively in the liver until an acute haemolytic crisis is triggered, producing icterus and port-wine coloured urine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Excess (not deficient) dietary molybdenum instead protects against copper poisoning by reducing hepatic copper storage — the opposite predisposing factor.
  • Sheep are, in fact, notably susceptible to dietary copper levels, being described as especially prone to copper poisoning.
  • Sheep are specifically highlighted as especially prone to copper poisoning, not exempted in favour of cattle alone.
Know More
  • Excess dietary molybdenum instead causes its own toxic syndrome in cattle called teart or peat scours.
  • The bluish-black kidney lesion, 'gun-metal kidney', is characteristic of chronic copper poisoning.
  • Treatment of copper poisoning includes d-penicillamine, calcium versenate and ammonium tetrathiomolybdate.
  • Bedlington terriers have a separate, genetic cause of excessive hepatic copper storage.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Which of the following statements correctly identifies a shared toxic mechanism between pentavalent arsenate and dinitro herbicide compounds?

_aimcq_options.text: Both are known uncouplers of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
Both act exclusively on GABA receptors

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both are known uncouplers of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation

Both pentavalent arsenate and dinitro herbicide compounds are known uncouplers of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

Correct Option Explanation

Uncoupling this process converts cellular energy production into heat rather than usable ATP; in dinitro herbicide poisoning this manifests as severe hyperthermia, illustrating a shared underlying biochemical mechanism across two structurally very different toxicant classes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates and carbamates, not arsenate or dinitro herbicides.
  • Vitamin K antagonism is the mechanism of anticoagulant rodenticides, unrelated to either arsenate or dinitro herbicides.
  • GABA receptor action is the mechanism of avermectins (ivermectin, milbemycin), not shared by arsenate or dinitro herbicides.
Know More
  • Trivalent arsenic separately reacts with the sulphydryl group of lipoic acid, inhibiting a different set of enzymes from pentavalent arsenate's uncoupling action.
  • 2,4,5-T ('Agent Orange') was used as a defoliant in the Vietnam War, a distinct herbicide from the dinitro class.
  • Paraquat, a different herbicide, instead causes selective lung toxicity via oxidative radical generation.
  • Sodium thiosulphate can be given orally and intravenously in arsenic poisoning treatment.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Regarding the enzyme responsible for detoxifying cyanide to thiocyanate, which statement is correct?

_aimcq_options.text: Rhodanase in the liver converts cyanide to non-toxic thiocyanate
Cytochrome P450 alone fully detoxifies cyanide with no residual toxicity risk
There is no enzymatic pathway for cyanide detoxification

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rhodanase in the liver converts cyanide to non-toxic thiocyanate

Cyanide is metabolised by rhodanase in the liver to the non-toxic compound thiocyanate.

Correct Option Explanation

The half-life for this conversion is 20 minutes to 1 hour; this natural detoxification pathway explains why tolerance can develop with repeated sub-lethal exposure, as seen in the potassium cyanide chronicity factor example (0.04).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acetylcholinesterase is unrelated to cyanide detoxification; it is instead the enzyme targeted by organophosphates and carbamates.
  • Cytochrome P450 is not identified as the enzyme responsible for cyanide-to-thiocyanate conversion in this source; rhodanase is specifically named for this role.
  • An enzymatic detoxification pathway clearly does exist for cyanide, contrary to a claim that no such pathway exists.
Know More
  • Sodium nitrite converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, which then complexes with cyanide to form cyanmethaemoglobin, aiding treatment.
  • Sodium thiosulphate supplies additional sulphur to support the rhodanase-mediated detoxification reaction.
  • Cyanide-poisoned exhaled air has a characteristic bitter almond smell.
  • Cyanide's primary mechanism is binding the ferric iron of cytochrome oxidase, blocking cellular respiration.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: The black light (UV) test, used in diagnosing aflatoxin contamination of feed, relies on which observation?

_aimcq_options.text: Bright greenish-yellow fluorescence of contaminated feed under UV light
Complete absence of any colour change under UV light
Red fluorescence specific to lead-contaminated feed
A colour change visible only under standard daylight

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bright greenish-yellow fluorescence of contaminated feed under UV light

The black light test for aflatoxin contamination shows bright greenish-yellow fluorescence under UV light.

Correct Option Explanation

This rapid screening method complements laboratory confirmation of aflatoxin contamination in feeds, which are typically produced by Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus growing under warm, moist storage conditions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The test specifically relies on the presence, not absence, of a distinctive fluorescent colour change under UV light.
  • Red fluorescence is not the finding associated with aflatoxin contamination; the characteristic colour is greenish-yellow.
  • The black light test specifically requires UV light, not standard daylight, to reveal the diagnostic fluorescence.
Know More
  • Hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate has high affinity for aflatoxins and can adsorb them in contaminated feed.
  • Aflatoxin toxicity order is B1 > G1 > B2 > G2, with B1 being most significant in mouldy feeds.
  • Aflatoxin B1 and B2 are excreted in milk as the related metabolites M1 and M2.
  • Most sensitive species to aflatoxin include rabbits, ducklings, minks, trout, dogs, turkeys and small pigs.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Shen Nung, regarded as the father of Chinese medicine, is historically credited with

_aimcq_options.text: Tasting 365 herbs and writing a treatise on herbal poisons around 2696 BC
Founding modern toxicology through chemical-biological correlation
Discovering the mechanism of action of curare
Issuing the first known law against poisoning in Rome

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tasting 365 herbs and writing a treatise on herbal poisons around 2696 BC

Shen Nung (2696 BC), the father of Chinese medicine, tasted 365 herbs and wrote a treatise on herbal poisons.

Correct Option Explanation

This represents one of the earliest documented systematic approaches to cataloguing plant toxicity in the history of toxicology, predating many other milestones such as Dioscorides's classification of poisons and Rome's early poison laws.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Founding modern toxicology through chemical-biological correlation is credited to M.J.B. Orfila, a much later (19th century) historical figure, not Shen Nung.
  • Discovering the mechanism of action of curare is credited to Claude Bernard, an entirely different historical contributor from Shen Nung.
  • The first known law against poisoning was issued by Sulla in Rome in 82 BC, a much later event than Shen Nung's era.
Know More
  • Pedanius Dioscorides (40-90 AD) classified poisons as animal, plant or mineral and recognised the value of emetics.
  • Maimonides wrote the 'Treatise on Poisons and Their Antidotes' during the Middle Ages.
  • The term 'mithridatic' (antidote) derives from King Mithridates VI of Pontus.
  • Paracelsus is famed for the dose-response principle that 'the dose makes the poison'.

posts.post_title: Which of the following statements about the…
posts.post_content: Occupational fatalities from parathion have specifically been documented following which route of exposure?

Correct Answer: Skin absorption

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chemical-related, animal-related and environment-related factors

Toxicity is modified by three broad categories of factors: chemical-related, animal-related and environment-related factors.

Correct Option Explanation

Chemical-related factors include dose, route, solubility and chemical/physical properties; animal-related factors include species, age, sex, size, nutritional and health status; environment-related factors include temperature, humidity and season.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Chemical structure alone does not capture the full picture — animal-related and environment-related factors are equally documented as important modifiers of toxicity.
  • Coat colour and breed registry status are not identified as toxicologically significant modifying factors in this framework; genuine animal-related factors include species, age and nutritional status.
  • Toxicity is explicitly not fixed — it is demonstrably modified by numerous documented factors across these three broad categories.
Know More
  • Very young and very old animals are generally more susceptible due to immature or declining detoxification/excretory capacity.
  • Cats show poor glucuronic acid conjugation, a species-related enzyme factor affecting susceptibility.
  • Rabbits possess the enzyme atropinase, conferring species-specific resistance to atropine.
  • High temperature increases parathion toxicity while low temperature increases malathion toxicity in mice, illustrating an environment-related factor.
